name: Muse-Glimmer-30B + OpenCode — private Apache-2.0 coding agent
description: A coding agent, not a chat window. OpenCode runs in this container with the repository, the terminal and the file tree in front of it, and Meta's Muse-Glimmer-30B on the GPU next to it does the thinking. Open the service URL, sign in, and give it work: it reads files, greps, edits, runs commands and shows you the diff before you keep it. Nothing to install locally and no third party sees the code or the conversation. Muse-Glimmer is the permissively licensed option: Apache-2.0, so anything you build on top of it is unencumbered. It scores 76.0 on SWE-bench Verified, 51.2 on SWE-bench Pro and 75.5 on MCP Atlas — that last figure is the one to weigh here, because it is a tool-use benchmark and an agent is nothing but a long chain of tool calls. Choose this template when your work leans on MCP servers and long tool chains; for raw coding strength the sibling Qwen3.8-27B template scores higher. Context is 131K tokens, and the model is natively multimodal, so screenshots, diagrams and photographed stack traces go straight into the session. Reasoning is graded through the system prompt rather than a parameter, so the workspace is seeded with an AGENTS.md containing `Reasoning strength: high` — edit that line to low, medium or xhigh; the card recommends high or xhigh for coding and agentic work. Sampling follows the card: temperature 1.0 and top_p 0.95 are set in OpenCode's provider config, and top_k 64 is applied server-side by vLLM because the OpenAI-compatible client cannot send it. HOW IT IS PUT TOGETHER: one container, one payment. vLLM serves the model on 127.0.0.1 only — the raw OpenAI-compatible API is never published, so there is no unauthenticated endpoint to find — and OpenCode's own server is the single exposed port. OpenCode is pinned to one release, downloaded to your bucket on first launch and reused after that, and it is configured with vllm as the ONLY provider, so no model in the picker can send your code off this box. It runs on the CPU; the whole GPU stays with the model. TWO REQUIREMENTS AT LAUNCH, both enforced by the startup script rather than discovered later. First, set OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD (12+ characters). This is not the same kind of login as a chat UI: OpenCode's tools run shell commands and write files in this container, HTTP basic auth is the only access control its server has, and it is off unless the password is set — so an unset password means anyone who finds the URL gets a shell for the rest of the paid window. With it set, every route answers 401 without credentials: the UI, the REST API and the event stream. The username defaults to `opencode` and can be changed with OPENCODE_SERVER_USERNAME. Second, select a persistent-storage bucket. It holds four things that make relaunching cheap and continuous: the 34 GB of model weights, the OpenCode binary, OpenCode's sessions and message history, and — the one that matters most — /data/outputs/workspace-muse, the project directory the agent edits. The node builds a fresh container on every launch, so without a bucket the weights re-download inside your paid window and the code the agent wrote is destroyed on stop; the container refuses to start rather than let that happen. Bring code in and take it out through the bucket. Shell commands ask for approval before they run and edits inside the workspace do not; change that, or add MCP servers, project instructions and agents, by dropping an opencode.json or editing AGENTS.md in the workspace — project config wins over the node-managed global config, which is rewritten on every launch. Ask for exactly ONE GPU: the model runs with tensor-parallel size 1 and cannot use a second card, which would simply be billed while idle.
outcome: Open a browser and put an Apache-2.0 coding agent to work on a persistent workspace — strong tool use, model on your own GPU.

workflows.name: Weights, workspace and history bucket
workflows.description: Not a workflow. This entry exists so the launch wizard offers the bucket picker: nodes-dashboard gates that picker on workflows[].length > 0 (templateNeedsBucketPicker in src/services/template-launch.ts). The bucket holds the model weights, the OpenCode binary, OpenCode's session history and the workspace the agent edits — without it the container refuses to start. The graph is deliberately empty and the container ignores COMFY_WORKFLOW entirely. Delete this once the node exposes a declarative persistence field.

requiredResources.description: ONE CUDA GPU with at least 40 GB of VRAM. The model is 29.8 GB in FP8 and the launch script gives vLLM 90% of the card. KV cache is unusually cheap here — only 13 of the 52 layers use full attention and the other 39 are capped by a 2048-token sliding window — so a 48 GB card comfortably holds the full 131K context, and a 141 GB H200 holds several long agent sessions at once. OpenCode is pinned to the CPU on purpose, so nothing competes with the model for VRAM. Ask for one card and not several: the model runs tensor-parallel size 1, a single-GPU process cannot spill onto a second device, and the extra card would be billed while idle. Staying on one GPU also keeps this template clear of the node's multi-GPU gap, where service containers get Docker's default 64 MB /dev/shm and no ipc=host.
